gathering on the traditional territory of the neutral Anishinaabe and Haudenosaunee peoples.
We recognize our responsibility to serve as stewards for the land and honor the original
caretakers who came before us. Our community is enriched by the enduring knowledge and deep-rooted
traditions of the diverse First Nations, Métis and Inuit in Kitchener today. Before we begin
this afternoon's meeting, I'd like to take a moment to recognize a few upcoming periods of
observance during the month of June. First, I'd like to acknowledge that June 6 commemorates
five years since the deadly attack on our London family. We continue to hold them in our hearts
and stand with communities across our region and country in remembering the three generations lost
to a cowardly act of hate. Moments like this remind us of the responsibility we all share
to challenge hate, foster understanding, and build a community where everyone feels safe and valued.
It is in that context that we continue to see the impacts of hate in our communities today.
Just weeks ago, a deadly attack at a mosque in San Diego claimed the lives of three people
in what authorities are investigating as a possible hate-motivated act. And in the coming
days, the Centre for Mutual Wellbeing, formerly known as the Coalition of Muslim Women, will
release its Snapshot of Hate report on June 6th. This report is an important reminder that Islamophobia
and other forms of hate continue to affect people across Ontario. As a Council and as a community,
we must remain committed to listening, learning, and taking meaningful action to address hate in
all its forms. That commitment to building a community where people feel safe, respected,
and included is reflected in how we recognize and celebrate the diversity of our city.
June is also a time to recognize Seniors Month, National Indigenous History Month, and Pride
Month.
In that spirit, I'd like to begin by recognizing Seniors Month.
June is a time to recognize and celebrate the contributions of older adults in our community.
This year's theme, Let's Get Moving, highlights the importance of staying active, engaged,
and connected as we age.
Across Kitchener, there are many opportunities for older adults to take part in programs and events that support wellness, learning, and social connection.
Seniors play an important role in shaping Kitchener as volunteers, mentors, leaders, and neighbours, and their experiences and perspectives strengthen our city.
Throughout Seniors Month, we also take time to celebrate these contributions and recognize outstanding community leaders through initiatives like the Senior of the Year Award.
This year's 2026 Senior of the Year Award will be presented at a special invitation-only event with the 13 nominees and their families on Wednesday, June the 10th.
It's also an opportunity to reflect on how we continue to build a community where older adults feel supported, connected, and able to age with dignity, independence, and a strong sense of belonging.
As we recognize the contributions of seniors in our community, we also take this time to reflect on the deeper histories that shape our city.
In a city like Kitchener, built on diverse stories, it's important to recognize the ones that came first.
The histories and contributions of First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples are a fundamental part of who we are as a community today.
As we mark National Indigenous History Month, it is time to reflect on that history and what it means for how we move forward together.

It is also a time to acknowledge the ongoing legacy of colonialism and the injustices, including displacement, forced assimilation, and systemic discrimination that continue to impact Indigenous communities.

Here in Kitchener, we're on the traditional territory of the neutral Anishinaabe and Haudenosaunee peoples, recognizing that history is an important part of understanding who we are as a community and how we should continue to move forward on our journey toward reconciliation.
It is also a time to listen, to listen to the voices of Indigenous peoples, to learn from their experiences, and to acknowledge the impacts of the past that continue to create inequities today.
Across our city, Indigenous residents, artists, knowledge keepers, and leaders are making important contributions to our community.
Their work, creativity, and leadership help make Kitchener a stronger and more inclusive place for everyone.
As a city, we remain committed to continuing the work of reconciliation.
That work takes time. It means building relationships based on respect, supporting Indigenous voices, and taking meaningful action.
As part of that ongoing work, we will be taking an important step forward this summer with the creation of an Indigenous Peoples Gathering Space in Victoria Park.
It will be a dedicated ceremonial fire space developed in partnership with local Indigenous communities, creating a place for gathering, reflection, and cultural practice.
This month also includes an opportunity to come together as a community.
June 21st is National Indigenous Peoples Day.
Celebrated on the summer solstice, it holds spiritual significance for many Indigenous peoples.
And I encourage everyone to attend community events and connect with the work of local Indigenous organizations.
As we continue this work together, I also encourage everyone to take part throughout the month by attending local events,
supporting Indigenous artists and businesses, and taking time to learn more about the history of this land
and the people who have called it home since time immemorial.
That same commitment to inclusion and belonging carries into how we also recognize Pride Month.
A sense of belonging is something we all share or long for.
It's the feeling of being able to show up as yourself, knowing you're respected, supported, and valued by the community around you.
In Kitchener, creating that kind of community is something we're committed to building every day.
As we mark Pride Month this June, we take time to celebrate the 2SLGBTQIA plus community,
the people, stories and contributions that help shape our city and recognize the ongoing efforts to ensure everyone can live safely and authentically.
But belonging doesn't happen on its own.
It's something we create together through the way we treat one another, the spaces we
build and the choices we make as a community.
Kitchener is committed to fostering a culture of inclusion where neighbours look out for
one another, where differences are welcomed and where everyone has the opportunity to
participate fully in community life.
That commitment shows up in big ways and small ones, in policies and programs and in everyday
acts of inclusion and respect.
Each of us has a role to play in that work.
Whether it's speaking up, offering support or simply choosing kindness, our individual
actions help shape a city and a world where people can live without a fear of discrimination
or exclusion and where everyone has the freedom to be who they are.
We see that commitment reflected in the strength of Kitchener's 2SLGBTQIA plus community.
Local artists, advocates and organizations like TriPiRite continue to lead with resilience,
and creativity, helping to build spaces where people feel seen and connected.
This spirit will be on full display at the Tribe Pride Festival on June 6 at Victoria Park,
where the community will gather to celebrate, connect, and show their pride and support.
Events like the Tribe Pride are a powerful reminder of the importance of visibility, community, and joy.
As we mark Pride in Kitchener and raise the Pride flag at City Hall, as we did this morning,
we do so with both celebration and purpose.
We're recognizing how far we've come and reaffirming the work that still lies ahead.
Together, we can continue building a city and a world where everyone belongs.
